source: Holyoak & Koh (1987) Surface and structural similarity in analogical transfer, Memory & Cognition 15(4)
finding: The paper restates the Gick and Holyoak baseline for the radiation problem: about 10% solve it with no analogue, about 30% solve it after reading the military story with no hint, and about 75% after a hint to use the story.
numbers: Typical experiment: ~10% no analogue; ~30% analogue without hint; ~75% analogue with hint (citing Gick & Holyoak 1980, 1983).
quote: only about 30% of subjects generated this solution prior to receiving an explicit hint
limits: Secondary restatement of the 1980 numbers; exact per-experiment values vary (Bearman et al. cite 8% pre-hint for analogue plus two distracters).
agent_relevance: Retrieving and noticing the source is the bottleneck, not mapping. O7 should include an explicit step that prompts the agent to look for and use a prior analogue, not wait for it to be noticed.

source: Holyoak & Koh (1987) Experiment 1
finding: Spontaneous analogical transfer is large when the source was activated recently and is not a lab-only artifact. Students who had discussed the radiation problem in class 3-7 days earlier solved a new lightbulb problem by analogy without any hint, versus almost nobody in controls.
numbers: Analogy group n=21: 81% solved lightbulb problem, 86% solved radiation problem. Controls n=10: 10% on both. Difference significant (G2(1)=15.2, p<.001 reported for one test).
limits: Small n; source was a famous textbook problem; delay only days; demand characteristics were argued against by the filler design but not eliminated.
agent_relevance: Spontaneous transfer does happen when the source is in memory and the target cue matches. For an LLM agent, the source library must be loaded into context or retrieved, because the model will not reliably recall it unprompted.

source: Holyoak & Koh (1987) Experiment 2: surface versus structural similarity
finding: Retrieval of an analogue without a hint depends on BOTH surface similarity (laser vs ultrasound) and structural similarity (fragile glass vs insufficient intensity constraint). The two effects were about equal and additive. Once a hint was given, only structural similarity still mattered.
numbers: No hint: laser + fragile glass 69% convergence solutions; ultrasound + insufficient intensity 13%. Each factor significant at p<.05 (laser vs ultrasound G2=4.42; fragile vs insufficient G2=5.92), no interaction. With hint, total transfer: fragile glass 78% vs insufficient intensity 54% (p<.05); laser 68% vs ultrasound 64% (n.s.).
limits: One target problem; between-subject cells of modest size.
agent_relevance: Key discriminating result against pure systematicity: retrieval is surface-driven, mapping/use is structure-driven. An agent should expect cheap similarity search to favour surface matches and add a separate structure check after retrieval (guardrail against false analogies).

source: Holyoak & Koh (1987) background on Gick & Holyoak (1983) schema induction
finding: Two analogous stories plus a task to write how they are similar (forcing a mapping) induce an abstract schema and raise transfer. The paper uses this to argue that comparison makes an abstract schema that no longer needs the original stories.
numbers: Not given on this page; the page describes the design only (summarise each story, write similarities, then attempt the X-ray problem before and after a hint).
limits: Numbers for the 1983 study were not on the opened page; do not cite effect sizes from this line.
agent_relevance: Supports a step where the agent compares two or more solved cases and writes the shared principle before applying it to the new problem (O7 with more than one source).

source: Bearman, Ormerod & Ball (2002) A Negative Effect of Evaluation Upon Analogical Problem Solving (Lancaster paper)
finding: Telling people to EVALUATE source stories reduced later analogical transfer compared with telling them to summarise. A moderator that went the opposite way to what the authors predicted. Pre-hint solution was rare (8%) and post-hint success was best with summaries.
numbers: Exp 1 (n=18 per cell) post-hint success: evaluative 28% (with memory instruction) and 22% (without); summary 61% and 50%. Source processing the only reliable predictor (Wald=6.7, p=.009). Pre-hint only 6 of 72 (8%) solved. Exp 2: pre-hint 1.3%; evaluation effect replicated (cells 22% and 16% evaluative vs 50% and 50% non-evaluative as read from the table).
quote: evaluation was found to have a detrimental effect on transfer compared with control groups instructed to summarize
limits: Radiation problem only; new nuclear power station source; n=18 per cell; authors suggest evaluation focuses attention on some source elements at the expense of the ones needed for transfer. Many participants also forgot sources (27 of 72 forgot one or more).
agent_relevance: A critique or judge step on the source can hurt reuse. In the agent, extract the abstract solution principle from the source first (summary-like) and only then evaluate fit to the target.

source: Bearman, Ormerod & Ball (2002), memory for sources
finding: Participants forgot the structurally relevant sources far more than the irrelevant one. Surface-similar and conceptually similar sources were both forgotten much more often than a non-analogous source, which suggests that interference, not absence of mapping skill, limits transfer.
numbers: Of 72 participants, 27 forgot at least one source. Non-analogous source forgotten once; superficially similar source 16 times; conceptually similar source 14 times (chi2=12.8, p=.002).
limits: Cue forgetting measured by recall of stories; confounded with story position.
agent_relevance: Distractor look-alike cases in context can crowd out the right analogue. Keep the analogue pool small and labelled, and show the agent why each case is relevant.

source: Beveridge & Parkins (1987) Visual representation in analogical problem solving, Memory & Cognition 15(3)
finding: A boundary condition on a null result: Gick and Holyoak found diagrams did not help the radiation problem, but visual analogues do help if they depict the right problem-solution relation (converging strips) rather than an irrelevant picture. A cuing diagram inside the problem also helped.
numbers: Exp 1: control 0% solved; Red Adair story 14%; coloured-strips analogue 32% (chi2=7.8). Exp 2: strips analogue 95% versus Red Adair 75%; intensity diagram 82% vs strips 95%. Children: 12% without diagram after analogue, 23% with cuing diagram. Students after analogue without cuing diagram 82%; with diagram 94% (p<.02).
limits: Children data come from a different sample; sample sizes per cell not captured in the opened text.
agent_relevance: The format of the source matters: it should show the relational structure. For tool-using agents, a structured schema of the source solution may transfer better than a long narrative.

source: Alfieri, Nokes-Malach & Schunn (2013) Learning through case comparisons: a meta-analytic review (SREE 2011 conference abstract version from ERIC ED528947)
finding: Learning from comparing two or more cases beats other instruction. Effects were heterogeneous but stable across age, setting, experience.
numbers: 57 experiments, 336 tests, random effects d=.60 (95% CI .47 to .72) in this conference version; Q(56)=136.74, I2=59%. Fail-safe N 2,795 (experiments) and 5,244 (tests). The published 2013 article is reported by secondary sources as d=.50; I did not open it.
limits: This is the 2011 conference abstract, not the final paper; the d value changed in the published version (secondary report .50, unverified). Case comparison is wider than analogy: many studies are classroom science and maths.
agent_relevance: The overall benefit of comparing cases is large enough to justify a compare-two-cases step before solving, not just single-source retrieval.

source: Alfieri et al. (2013), moderators (conference version)
finding: Five of 15 moderators held up: content, principle, features, objective, lag. Learners gain most when asked ONLY to find similarities (not differences), when the features of at least one case are given, and when the principle is given AFTER the comparison. Immediate tests beat delayed ones, but there is no lag effect when the principle follows the comparison.
numbers: Comparison vs sequential presentation d=.37; vs control .69; vs non-analogous .82 (as read from a noisy table). Adults d=.53 (CI .42 to .64); adolescents d=.34 (CI -.01 to .68, k=4). Publication rank: top .59, second .73, conference .28.
limits: Table parsing from pdftotext is noisy; subgroup numbers should be re-checked against the published paper. Age, setting, experience, task type did not moderate.
agent_relevance: Design for O7: show the two cases side by side, ask for shared structure first, then state the principle, then apply. Do not ask for differences first.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models, Nature Human Behaviour (arXiv 2212.09196)
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) matched or beat college students on text matrix reasoning, letter strings and verbal analogies in zero-shot tests. Source of the claim 'emergent analogical reasoning'.
numbers: Digit Matrices: humans N=40; letter strings N=57; verbal analogies N=57; story analogies N=54 (UCLA undergraduates). GPT-3 above human average on most letter-string problem types. Digit Matrices zero-shot GPT-3 matched or exceeded human accuracy.
limits: Letter strings used the authors' own idea of correct answers; training-data overlap not excluded; only a text-davinci-003 snapshot and a GPT-4 preview.
agent_relevance: The headline baseline that later robustness papers challenge. Do not assume LLM analogy ability from standard benchmarks.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) story analogies (Gentner et al. materials)
finding: Structure mapping preference test: given a source story and two targets with matching first-order relations but only one with matching causal (higher-order) relations, humans chose the causal match; GPT-3 did so in near analogy but not significantly in far analogy. GPT-4 did better.
numbers: Humans N=54: t(53)=21.3 overall, 15 of 54 chose the analogous story on every trial. GPT-3: overall binomial p=.0005, near p=.0039, far p=.065 (not significant). GPT-3 vs humans: odds ratio 0.37, p=.0003. GPT-4 preliminary: nearly perfect in near, more robust in far.
limits: Only 18 story problems per condition; GPT-4 result was preliminary.
agent_relevance: The systematicity preference (relational over surface match) is partly present in LLMs but weaker for far, cross-domain pairs, which is exactly where O7 matters.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2023) Gick and Holyoak radiation problem replicated with GPT-3
finding: GPT-3 reproduced the human pattern in a qualitative test: alone it missed the convergence solution; after the general story it found it; with two distractor stories it missed it again; with a prompt to consider the earlier stories it found it.
numbers: Qualitative, single transcripts, no counts. Also tested the children's gumball/genie paradigm.
limits: Qualitative; not a statistical test; one run per condition. Only describes GPT-3.
agent_relevance: Direct match for the retrieval-versus-mapping split in humans: an explicit prompt to consider prior cases is what restored use. This supports an explicit 'consider the stored analogues' step.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) Using counterfactual tasks to evaluate the generality of analogical reasoning in LLMs (arXiv 2402.08955)
finding: On letter-string analogies with permuted or symbol alphabets, human accuracy stayed high while GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 dropped sharply. The authors argue the models rely on similarity to training data.
numbers: Across all alphabets and problem types: humans 0.753 (CI .734 to .773; 1,876 samples); GPT-3 0.488; GPT-3.5 0.350; GPT-4 0.452 (6,840 samples each). Humans (Prolific, 136 recruited, 2 rejected) constant over permutation level; the GPT models fall for permuted alphabets and again for symbol alphabets.
limits: Prolific sample scored higher than Webb's undergraduates; no chain-of-thought or reasoning models tested; counterfactual comprehension checks (CCC) were used to check the models knew the alphabet.
agent_relevance: Measured brittleness of mapping when surface form changes. Test any O7 implementation on surface-altered copies of the same relational problem.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2025) Evaluating the robustness of analogical reasoning in LLMs (arXiv 2411.14215)
finding: Extended version covering letter strings, digit matrices and story analogies. Failed to show robust transfer in GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on most variants. Digit-matrix result is a split: moving the blank breaks the models, replacing digits by symbols does not.
numbers: Digit matrices, mean accuracy [humans / GPT-3.5 / GPT-4]: Digits .715 / .813 / .810; Alt. Blank .771 / .480 / .477; Symbols .704 / .790 / .792. Human samples 1,550 (Digits), 1,000 each for the variants.
limits: Zero-shot, simple prompts only; no chain-of-thought and no reasoning models; GPT versions limited to 0613 snapshots.
agent_relevance: Not all surface changes hurt equally. Answer position and format cause failures that symbol identity does not: format brittleness is a risk separate from analogy skill.

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2025) story analogy robustness
finding: Webb's GPT-4 story-analogy result was biased by the order of the two answers, and dropped when the correct target story was paraphrased so it no longer matched the source sentence by sentence. Humans were less affected.
numbers: Original WHL data: GPT-4 89% (16/18) when Story A correct, 61% (11/18) when B correct. Replication: GPT-4 1.0 vs 0.72, total 0.86 (31/36); humans 0.78 (564/720) in both positions. Paraphrased correct target: GPT-4 0.86 to 0.72 (26/36); humans 0.78 to 0.70 (503/720).
limits: Only 18 problems; small GPT sample (36 trials); paraphrases written by the authors.
agent_relevance: A shortcut exists: sentence-level similarity can stand in for causal structure. For tests of structural matching, control for surface and position.

source: Stevenson, Pafford, van der Maas & Mitchell (2025) Can LLMs generalize analogy solving like children can? (arXiv 2411.02348)
finding: Children (7-9) and adults transfer letter-string analogy rules to Greek and symbol alphabets with no loss. All four LLMs lose accuracy as the domain moves away from Latin letters, so the LLMs generalise worse than the children in the far domain.
numbers: Mean accuracy Latin / Greek / Symbol: adults .88/.91/.89 (n=62); children .62/.66/.67 (n=41); Claude-3.5 .68/.62/.46; Gemma-2 27B .60/.39/.14; GPT-4o .85/.63/.48; Llama-3.1 405B .79/.74/.27 (n=54 runs each). Adults and children no significant alphabet effect (F=.95, .27); LLM alphabet effect p<.001.
limits: Short strings, simple rules; zero-shot; four LLMs. Rule-check task showed models can do successor_1 in the symbol list but fail on successor_2 and predecessor, so part of the drop is rule knowledge, not mapping.
agent_relevance: Even a model that does well on the standard case fails once the domain is unfamiliar. For O7 the agent should check that the relation operators work in the target domain before trusting the mapping.

source: Musker, Duchnowski, Milliere & Pavlick (2025) LLMs as models for analogical reasoning, J. Memory and Language 145
finding: Tasks requiring re-representation (mapping words to symbol patterns by semantic features such as is-mammal, number of legs). The best LLM matched human performance in the default condition, but differed from humans on control conditions.
numbers: Study 1: LLMs more sensitive to presentation order (Permuted Pairs) and misled by irrelevant semantic distractors, while humans were not. Study 2: the best model matched human performance in every condition and beat humans on compositional variants. Exact percentages are in figures that I did not extract.
limits: The paper's own stance: LLMs give a how-possibly, not how-actually, account. Exact numbers not read from tables here.
agent_relevance: Order and distractor sensitivity suggest the agent should present analogues in a canonical order and strip irrelevant semantic detail before mapping.

source: Musker et al. (2025), discussion of the counterfactual debate
finding: Summarises the dispute: Lewis and Mitchell read the counterfactual drop as lack of general analogy; Webb, Holyoak and Lu (2024) argue task demands unrelated to analogy (alphabet knowledge, format) explain it; Musker et al. use the competence-performance distinction and say both sides have support.
numbers: No new numbers.
limits: The Webb, Holyoak and Lu (2024) reply was not opened by this agent, only described here.
agent_relevance: Treat failures in unusual alphabets as possibly performance limits (token-level skills), and use chain-of-thought or tools for them, instead of concluding that analogy itself is missing.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners, ICLR 2024 (arXiv 2310.01714)
finding: Analogical prompting asks the model to recall relevant problems itself and then solve the target. It beats 0-shot CoT and often 3-5-shot CoT with fixed exemplars on math and code.
numbers: GSM8K accuracy, 0-shot / 0-shot CoT / 5-shot CoT / self-generated exemplars: GPT-3.5-turbo 75.0 / 75.8 / 76.7 / 77.8; text-davinci-003 14.8 / 50.3 / 54.0 / 61.0; PaLM2 60.8 / 78.2 / 80.7 / 81.7. MATH: GPT-3.5-turbo 33.0 / 33.9 / 34.9 / 37.3; PaLM2 27.1 / 29.8 / 34.3 / 34.8. Codeforces Acc@1 with GPT-3.5-turbo-16k: 0-shot 8%, 0-shot CoT 9%, 3-shot CoT 11%, self-generated exemplars 13%, self-generated knowledge+exemplars 15%.
limits: Gains on strong models are small (about 1 to 3 points on GSM8K); more tokens are generated; self-generated exemplars are not checked for correctness. Some numbers come from a table that pdftotext split into columns, so the column alignment is my reading.
agent_relevance: The only LLM method here that directly gives O7-like benefit. But it is a recall-then-solve prompt with no structural check, so it is closer to analogical retrieval than to structure mapping.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024), scale boundary
finding: Self-generated analogues work only when the base model is strong enough. At small scale, retrieved fixed exemplars beat self-generation, and small models produce invalid exemplars.
numbers: GSM8K, 0-shot CoT / 5-shot retrieved / self-generated: text-curie-001 2% / 3% / 2%; text-davinci-001 6% / 11% / 9%; text-davinci-002 22% / 47% / 48%; text-davinci-003 50% / 57% / 61%.
limits: Old base models; all numbers in the scaling table are for the original GPT-3 line.
agent_relevance: Use externally curated analogue stores for weaker sub-agents; use self-recall only with a strong model.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024), failure analysis
finding: A common failure was a generalisation gap: the generated exemplars were easier than the new problem, so the solution method did not carry over. Authors list higher inference cost as a limitation.
numbers: No count of failures was extracted.
limits: Qualitative error analysis.
agent_relevance: Add a check that the analogue is at least as hard and uses the same constraint structure as the target (the structural-constraint finding of Holyoak and Koh, b03).

source: Lewis & Mitchell (2024) replication of Webb et al. on original letter strings
finding: Partial replication of Webb on original letter strings: the GPT models did worse than humans in the replication, unlike the original, which reversed the headline. Part of the gap is that the replication humans did better than Webb's undergraduates.
numbers: Human accuracy in the replication was higher than Webb's undergraduates; GPT performance close to Webb's in aggregate but different by problem type. Overall human 0.753 vs GPT-3 0.488 in the full counterfactual set.
limits: Different participant pools (Prolific UK/US vs UCLA undergraduates) and protocols; the authors warn this may explain the difference.
agent_relevance: The claim that LLMs beat humans on analogy is sensitive to which humans were tested. Keep a human baseline and a robustness baseline in our own tests.

source: Gick & Holyoak (1980) Analogical problem solving, Cognitive Psychology 12, 306-355
finding: Founding study: subjects who read a military convergence story solved the radiation problem much more often when told to use it; without the hint the frequency of analogous solutions decreased markedly. Only the abstract record was seen via search, not the paper.
numbers: Secondary sources and Holyoak and Koh (1987) give about 10% (no analogue), 30% (analogue, no hint), 75% (hint). Other secondary sources report 76% to 92%.
limits: Not opened. The range of hint values depends on the experiment and on the story used.
agent_relevance: Same as b01. Cite only through the opened secondary until the primary is read.

source: Reeves & Weisberg (1994) The role of content and abstract information in analogical transfer, Psychological Bulletin
finding: Known review arguing for schema/abstraction combined with case-based content as the basis of transfer. Not opened; included as a pointer from memory only.
numbers: none
limits: Not read this session. Treat as unverified.
agent_relevance: Candidate for a later pass on the schema-versus-case debate.

source: Webb, Holyoak & Lu (2024) Evidence from counterfactual tasks supports emergent analogical reasoning (reply to Lewis & Mitchell)
finding: Described in Musker et al. as arguing that the counterfactual-task failure comes from non-analogy demands. Not opened; no URL recorded because the id could not be verified.
numbers: none
limits: Not read.
agent_relevance: Needs a pass before citing; its main point (task-demand confounds) is already covered through b18.

source: Bearman, Ormerod & Ball (2002) pre-hint baseline versus Gick & Holyoak (1980)
finding: Conceptual replication of the low pre-hint rate: 8% in Exp 1 (matching Gick & Holyoak Exp 4 with an analogue and two distracters) and a lower 1.3% in Exp 2, which the authors call a significant drop from the standard 8%.
numbers: Exp 1: 6 of 72 (8%). Exp 2: 1 participant (1.3%).
limits: They used a new source (nuclear power station), not the military story, so it is a conceptual rather than a direct replication.
agent_relevance: Spontaneous noticing is low and fragile across materials and procedures. Do not design around it.
